letters.desc: Existing customers face billions in cost shifts because utilities functionalize large-load connection infrastructure as transmission and spread it across the rate base. State commissions and FERC should require deposits, direct cost assignment, and tariff provisions that prevent this subsidy from flowing from ordinary customers to data center operators.
quotes: The consequences are higher prices for consumers and regulators at every level facing significant questions as to how to meet electricity demand growth while ensuring affordability and reliability.

large load customers often require new lines and substations at voltages of 138kV or higher. Mr. Jacobs explained that although such high-voltage connection facilities are essentially line extensions that the utility designs to serve a specific customer, the utilities socialize their costs by placing them into the transmission rate base.

the California Public Utilities Commission recently issued an interim order requiring new transmission-level customers seeking retail services to be responsible for the initial costs of all transmission facilities, rather than those costs being borne by ratepayers.

the Commission should order ComEd to collect deposits for the incremental costs of Large Demand Project Applicants or Customers, regardless of whether those costs are deemed by ComEd to be transmission costs or distribution costs.

letters.desc: Hopkins points to the Shapiro price cap as temporary protection that will expire in 2030, and urges FERC to act before that deadline to prevent further cost increases for Pennsylvania residential customers.
quotes: act before the Shapiro price cap expires in 2030. The cap has provided temporary protection for Pennsylvania ratepayers. Without action, costs will increase even more.

letters.desc: NMPRC emphasizes that ratepayers cannot be required to finance new generation or infrastructure without state review of costs and necessity.
quotes: FERC cannot require New Mexico ratepayers to finance new generation or infrastructure that has not gone through New Mexico's planning and approval requirements, whether initiated through the IRP process, certificate proceedings, or any of the other regulatory pathways the NMPRC uses to review and approve new resources.

letters.org: Pennsylvania Office of Consumer AdvocateDelaware Division of the Public Advocate
letters.desc: The overarching theme of the filing is protecting residential electricity consumers in Pennsylvania and Delaware from paying higher rates or receiving less reliable service because of large load interconnection. The filers propose a multi-layer protection package covering cost assignment, minimum charges, contract terms, and financial collateral.
quotes: The Joint Consumer Advocates seek to ensure that these ratepayers do not pay higher rates for less reliable (i.e., inferior) service resulting from the interconnection of large loads that do not offset their load through the addition of timely, local, and adequate capacity resources.

The Joint Consumer Advocates support a package of ratepayer protections to the extent that the Commission finds them to be jurisdictional: 1) minimum contractual duration, renewal, and cancellation provisions; 2) minimum demand payments and demand ramping requirements; 3) financial collateral and guarantees.

The Joint Consumer Advocates support the establishment of clear contract terms regarding duration, renewal, and termination fees. Additionally, a minimum demand charge of 85% of forecasted peak demand at the conclusion of the ramp period would be reasonable.

letters.desc: Vistra opposes embedding large-load network upgrade costs in rate base because it shifts risk to existing ratepayers if a large load fails to materialize or consumes less than forecast. Participant funding avoids this risk entirely.
quotes: The third option, to contrast, creates a significant risk of cost shifts to other customers if a large load customer fails to materialize, consumes less energy than intended, or ceases operation sooner than anticipated.

letters.desc: The filer argues that cost allocation decisions must account for their impact on all retail customers. They note that rolled-in rates can actually lower costs for existing customers because large loads dilute the per-unit share, while direct assignment risks balkanizing the network and raising costs for non-data-center customers.
quotes: regardless of how the Commission decides to allocate the costs of network upgrades, it must consider how the effect of its action or inaction affects all customers—not just large load customers.
